utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As there was mention yesterday about the OSCE report, Mr. Ryneveld quoted an order, an order which was, he says, sent to me. I don't use the book, but I looked at the OSCE report. The original OSCE mission's report on the 12th of February, 1999, I have it here in its entirety, says that the security forces conducted a joint operation against the KLA in Jeskovo. For the KLA, it was reported that they attacked the area of Zlociste, using mortars and heavy machine-guns. It also states that the Prizren Regional Centre commented this and said that the KLA infiltrated itself into Jeskovo which had been a previously abandoned village, one week previously, and the inhabitants of Hoca Zagradska informed the OSCE of their concern because of this KLA move. And it was told to the KLA that the local security forces viewed their presence in the area as a provocation. So we can see that the village had been abandoned of the civilians, that they had left, and we can see what had happened. They limited the combat operations on -- at Jeskovo with other villages which were not damaged. That is the report of the 11th of March. It is several pages long. I can hand it in to you. And another report of the 12th of March, which was quoted yesterday by Mr. Ryneveld, it states that during the operation in Jeskovo on the 11th of March, 500 inhabitants of the village of Ljubicevo left and that it was the subject of a search by the army of Yugoslavia, that the police invited the OSCE to visit Jeskovo, with the quotation quoted yesterday by Mr. Ryneveld about the persons killed belonging to the KLA, wearing uniforms and carrying weapons. And the next quotation which he did not quote, the next sentence is that there were mortar weapons found with ammunition, et cetera, and this was in some boxes, and it was assessed that firing came from the mortars recently. And the next paragraph said that the OSCE noticed that the KLA had dug new trenches near Mamusa, et cetera, et cetera. So those, then, are the reports about their work on the 11th of March and 12th of March in their entirety. You can take them, if you like. And as I mentioned them and quoted them, the first number of these documents is SFR 208/99, and the other document is numbered -- I can't quite find it here now, but it says, as this was provided in Vienna and the subject is the OSCE Kosovo Verification Mission report on the activities of the 12th of March. So it applies to the 11th and 12th of March. These are the reports not from the book "Under Orders" but from the original report which write about what I brought forth here. That's all from me. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to hand them in.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. Here they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Certainly the second part of the quotation I recognise from the book. I don't know about the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I know nothing about the first. All this shows is the desirability of these exhibits being produced for witnesses when they're being cross-examined. We will have a look at the first one, of course, in due course and see if there are any observations we want to make on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And then we'll consider exhibiting it. As far as this witness is concerned, the first point is that there is no need to produce a new copy of the exhibits. We can simply cross out the passages which we've excluded and the report can go in in that way, to save time. And the second point is that we must finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So if you would organise your examination-in-chief in order to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will be as brief as I can, consistent with making its content not only clear or clearer to Your Honours but also to those following the trial elsewhere. So far as exhibits are concerned, before I turn to Mr. Coo's exhibits that relate to himself and his report, deal with the previous witness or earlier witness, Sir Peter de la Billiere, and produce through this witness a list of the documents that were served or provided to the witness because that was a matter that was in dispute. So we have a list to be produced, please, of the documents provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It will take only a minute to produce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Coo, does this document, which we would ask to be exhibited, contain a list of the items provided to Sir Peter de la Billiere on two occasions; the initial occasion and then, overleaf, documents provided for a 2nd of May meeting and one document provided for -- on the 14th of May by mail, together with certain indications of the purposes for which the documents were being provided?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd need to see a copy of the list, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this as a list of documents I put together and gave to General Sir Peter de la Billiere to assist him in the drafting of his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turning to your own materials --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask, actually, that we produce the two reports now and find a way of producing the exhibits compendiously.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you prepared two reports, the second of which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt. Let us deal with the documents provided to General de la Billiere first and get a number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This list will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 317.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The position on reports, Mr. Coo, is that you prepared the first report which was filed on the 16th of May of this year, and then as to the later report, it was prepared in two versions, a first and an amended version, the amended version being filed, I think, on the 2nd of July of 2002.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask, so I don't overlook it, that they are each produced subject, of course, to the deletions that were ordered yesterday being dealt with in hand.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Part I of the report will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 318.1, and Part II will be 318.2, with a copy of the transcript attached, signifying the changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you then provide additional supporting materials to your second report, Mr. Coo, on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is there is a large number of files of exhibits. I'm not sure how many altogether. There's 15 binders altogether, two of which have already been produced through Sir Peter de la Billiere, and I would ask that we find a way of producing them compendiously.

utterances.text: The way we've done it in the past is to have a single exhibit number and then tabs within that number; and they're all tabbed, as I understand it.

utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.text: Could we have the two exhibit numbers, please.

utterances.text: The binders will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 319.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it will have to be two exhibit numbers because there's one attached to Part I and there's another attached to Part II.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And Prosecutor's Exhibit 320.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In those circumstances, may the additional materials provided to the second expert report, if they're outside the tab -- no. Very well. Nothing. The witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The only one I can think of is the blue book, which I have read, the OSCE blue book, which should be produced probably separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are going to be half a dozen other separate documents that will be produced right at the end, they having come into our possession very recently. The blue book, then, maybe that could be given a separate exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'd ask that the usher has available, but not to go to the overhead projector immediately, a copy of the first report in the format that the Chamber has it, and from time to time I'll ask her to lay particular pages on the overhead projector so that the passages being referred to can be read.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I now turn, Mr. Coo, to the structure of your first report. And I don't ask this to be laid on the overhead projector. It begins with an executive summary. And if you can, in just a couple of sentences, tell us, please, how at the end of the exercise you were able to sum matters up. And it may be for this you'll want one exhibit to look at or to have on the overhead projector, and it's the only one we'll be taking in any sense out of order, and it comes from Annex D1, page 53 of part A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And there are complementary copies of the exhibits we are producing for the Chamber, if that will be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Do I take it the tab in each number is 53, since that's what we've been working off?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The tab -- this is Annex 1, the end of Part I, section A, and there is the table showing the organisation of military forces. So the tab reference would be, for this tab -- this is within the report and doesn't have a tab reference, I'm afraid. It's page 53 of A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Isn't this page 54?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the page numbers have changed, it's because Your Honour is reading from the slightly amended version that has the tab references in it that has thrown the numbering out. I'll try and read in the corrected page references. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, then, in a couple of sentences, your conclusions from the materials you looked at for your first report.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was able to determine from a review of documentation covering Part I of the report that the structure of the armed organisations in Kosovo consisted of -- or the structure of the armed organisations in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia was comprised of the regular army, or the VJ, the military territorial units which formed military territorial combat units and administered conscription on behalf of the VJ. There were the police forces known by the B/C/S acronym MUP, and what can be termed or grouped under the collective title local defence forces. And local defence forces comprised of the two types of forces I've just mentioned, VJ and military territorial units forming the military, and also the MUP, and a collection of other units which included civilian defence units and civilian protection units, along with armed civilians. Furthermore, I was able to determine the means of commanding, the official means of commanding these organisations, and some of this is shown on the ELMO at the moment. At the top is the Supreme Defence Council, headed by the president of the FRY, and the report shows with reference to legislation and the constitution, and additionally to VJ doctrinal manuals, that indeed the command of the military is in the hands of the FRY president. The top of the VJ's chain of command is the VJ General Staff headed by the Chief of the General Staff who, at the time in 1999, was General Ojdanic. Under the General Staff were three armies. Of concern to Kosovo was the VJ 3rd Army headed by, in 1999, General Pavkovic, who had formerly been commander of the Pristina Corps. Subordinate to General Pavkovic, or subordinate to the 3rd Army, were the Pristina Corps commanded, in 1999, by General Lazarevic, and the Pristina Military District. The Pristina Military District represents the military territorial organisation, and that organisation had responsibility covering two areas. One was administering the conscription on behalf of the regular army, the VJ. The other was forming combat units during times of crisis, and those combat units would operate within the chain of command which I'm outlining. The military district was subdivided into military sectors, of which there were five in Kosovo, and within those military sectors were military departments and military territorial units. Pristina Corps was subdivided into a number of brigades. This number increased during 1999, during the state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The diagram on the overhead projector shows dotted line connections between the Pristina military district and the Pristina Corps and between the military departments and the brigades forming part of the Pristina Corps. Could you explain, please?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The Pristina Military District, during peacetime, according to the documentation, had a formal reporting chain to the 3rd Army and would administer conscription and other aspects of the reserve system on behalf of the 3rd Army. During times of crisis when the Pristina Military District formed combat units, those combat units would be in some cases subordinated to VJ brigades. And when subordinated in this manner, they would report on their activities to the VJ brigade to which they were subordinate. In addition, I've also seen documentation showing the Pristina Military District reporting to the Pristina Corps, demonstrating that on some occasions it was being -- suggesting that on some occasions that the Pristina Military District was responding to the direction of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. One last question before we move to the first section of your report and look at one or two things in detail. You speak of the combat units formed by the military district. Of what were those combat units themselves formed?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military district combat units were formed from people with obligations for reserve service and conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we turn, then, now to section A of your report, and I think there are some three or four pages we may look at in a little detail of this. We can see on the first page that you have summarised section A, which is about the organisation and command and control of the VJ itself, the army of Yugoslavia. You needn't place page 1 on the overhead projector, but can you, in a sentence, summarise the effect of part A of your report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part A made use of a large amount of material, including the constitution, the FRY constitution, and the federal laws on defence and the federal law on the VJ. In addition, it relied heavily on a VJ manual known as the Manual on Command and Control, and that manual was intended for the, among other things, the training of senior officers within the VJ. From the documentation, I was able to determine the official structure of the VJ and its means of command. The structure is relatively simple, and that was covered, I think, in the previous chart. The means Blank page inserted to make pagination between French and English transcript correspond 24 25 of commanding the VJ are well laid out in the constitution, legislation, and the doctrine, and it clearly states that command begins at the level of the FRY president.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to page 14 of the section - that's 14 out of 53 - where you set out Article 48 of the FRY law on defence, which states that the state organs and organisations not cited in this law shall exercise their rights and duties in the field of the defence of the country in accordance with the constitution of the FRY federal law and other federal regulations and carry out the duties stipulated in the country's defence plan and decisions of the federal government on preparations for defence. That article sustains your conclusion in paragraph 26, namely?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This article shows to me that the defence of the -- of Yugoslavia was a federal responsibility. And in addition to the regular military forces, the VJ, other units were involved and other organs were involved in -- in defence of the country, and these are captured in Article 48, which suggests to me that their involvement came under federal responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. You -- in your report, you deal with various topics. We needn't break them down, but by page 23, you're in a sector headed Principles of Command, something upon which I think you focused and on which you have written. And on page 23, you cite Article 3 of the law on the VJ. And explain that -- perhaps you'd read it out for us and then explain its significance in simple terms for those who don't have military backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 3 from the law on the VJ, the federal law on the VJ, states that: "Command in the army shall be based on the principles of unity of command with respect to the uses of forces and materiel, the single command concept, and the obligation to carry out decisions, commands, and orders of a superior officer." Two of those principles, the unity of command and the single command concept I've covered in detail in section A. The other principle, that of following the order of -- orders of superior officers is also covered but less directly. This framing of these principles in the law on the VJ captures in legal terms what the VJ recognised in its doctrine and was mandated to practice in its doctrine. The principle of unity of command refers to -- is in essence an efficiency measure, and its purpose is to ensure that all forces operating in defence of the country are operating on command principles, using common systems, and that would include the VJ and the MUP operating jointly on combat operations. The aim of the unity -- principle of unity of command would be to ensure that the -- both the MUP and the VJ and any other forces operating together were using systems with as much commonness as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turn to paragraph 47, a couple of pages further on, please. And you may want to link this with paragraph 50 in concluding what I want you to say on this particular topic. Paragraph 47 has you dealing with continuity as a fundamental principle of command. Can you explain that? It's there in writing, but a word of explanation.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Continuity is fundamental to military operations. A commander has to know at all times what's going on in his area of responsibility; and to do that, there has to be continuity in, among other things, the reporting of events up the chain of command. So units engaged in operations on the ground are obligated to report on their activities up through the chain of command to ensure that commanders are aware of what's happening and can act on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And also does this take care of the potential for breakdown in communication if one link in the chain goes, for example, by death or for other reason disappearance of a particular commander?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It ensures that, having awareness of this principle, the VJ would operate, would ensure that it had measures in place to address the possibility of a commander being killed, and they make it clear who is next in line to command should that happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 50 on page 26, please. You speak here of the dynamic between the FRY president and the Chief of the General Staff. And the footnote refers to the Manual on Command and Control, which we don't need to pull out. Just explain the citation and the significance, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- this extract from the Manual on Command and Control reinforces the constitution and the federal laws on defence and on the VJ in which it is stated that the FRY president commands the VJ and specifically through the Chief of the General Staff. And here it is -- here are the contents of the constitution and the laws encapsulated in a VJ doctrinal manual on command and control, showing that VJ officers who are trained using this manual would be trained in that very -- in those very -- in the very constitution and the laws on defence in the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me turn over to the foot of page 50 but in substance to page 51. At the foot of page 50 of sector A, we see you've turned to a topic headed "Promotions, Commendations, and Appointments." The page number may have slipped for those with the slightly amended version. So it will either be -- beg your pardon. It will either be 50 or 51. No. I'm -- I think I have a page out of order, so I think it may be page 49, which makes more sense. If you would go to page 49, please, and to paragraph 100.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Page 50, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 50. Paragraph 100, in any event. And this is within -- it makes appropriate sense -- the sector on Regulations on the Application of International Laws of War. Paragraph 100 picks up some instructions from the Regulations on the Application of the International Laws of War in the Armed Forces of the SFRY. The first passage, the first five lines sets out the personal responsibility of any officer. Can you just amplify that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an internal regulation in use by the VJ, and it shows that what might colloquially be known as trigger-pullers, while they bear responsibility for the crimes they commit, there's also command responsibility for those crimes if the proper action is not taken, and this extract clearly demonstrates to me what that command responsibility is. And commanders in the VJ would have an obligation to be aware of the contents of this regulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we go to page 51 - it may be 52 now - paragraph 105. We see your conclusions on this section, I think probably the longest of the sections in either report. And you set out that the VJ was, in 1998 and 1999, the professional, heavily armed organised military force with a well-established doctrine. We may have had this from someone else. Doctrine, is this something that you find in a book headed "Doctrine" or is doctrine something that can be discovered by considering all the written materials for any given army?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Doctrine is encompassed in all the written materials of an army. Academics may produce books called "Doctrine", but doctrine itself is integrated into the manuals and other publications and regulations which militaries have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your conclusion goes on, in paragraph 105, to deal with the military territorial organisation to which you've referred, how the VJ and those units operated within a clear constitutional, legal and regulatory framework in which a simple unbroken chain of command was derived, at the top of which command was President Milosevic under whose authority those military forces could operate. That was your conclusion, was it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, based on documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 106, you set out in writing the contents of the chart we first looked at, as with 107. And 108, you make this comment: "Commanding and controlling a force of that size demanded a functioning chain of command and clear direction. The VJ had and was mandated to employ commonly accepted Blank page inserted to make pagination between French and English transcript correspond 24 25 principles of command, the two most important of which were unity of command and singleness of command." We've touched on those topics. Does that remain your opinion?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You then set out the requirement for VJ and military territorial units to operate under precise legal provisions, to obey the law of armed conflict and international humanitarian law binding all military personnel; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ultimate authority and responsibility for military discipline being vested in the FRY president as commander of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we then turn to sector B, which is about 39 pages. It doesn't have a concluding summary, it has an opening summary on page 1. The topic is the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs, its organisation and command. Can you, in a couple of sentences, encapsulate your findings? We're only going to be taking the Chamber to some four references within this sector.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, from reviewing the documentation, it was -- it became clear to me that the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs, or the MUP, was organised, as were the VJ, in a very well-structured manner and had a -- a system of command, a means of command which had a basis in Serbian legislation, and internal regulations of the MUP also reflected that legislative basis. The organisation of the Serbian MUP was -- in basic terms, was structured along the following lines: It was broken down into two divisions; the state security division responsible for, in very general terms, counter-intelligence. It also had a special arm -- heavily armed uniformed unit called the Special Operations Unit, or the JSO, sometimes known by the unofficial term "Red Berets" or "Frenki's Boys." The other division within the MUP was the public security division, known by the acronym RJB. This contained what might be termed normal police, police responsible for criminal investigations and traffic. But it also contained two special units, the special anti-terrorist unit, or SAJ, and the special police unit, the PJP, both of which were heavily armed. The PJP was much larger than the SAJ and was armed and equipped along the lines of a military light infantry unit. It had, for example, mortars. The geographical structure of the MUP went along the lines of having Secretariats of Internal Affairs, or SUPs, of which there were seven in Kosovo. Kosovo was a special case, having between the SUP level and the ministry level in Belgrade a headquarters called the MUP staff for Kosovo, and that MUP staff was commanded by General Sreten Lukic. The MUP staff was responsible for coordinating the activities of the seven SUPs, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your part B of your report is broken out, dealing with various aspects of organisation, and having just dealt with the SUPs, if we go to about page 10, more materially to page 12. In dealing with the RJB within the SUPs, paragraph 17 you make a particular observation of potential significance in light of the evidence in the case concerning possible transfers. Could you explain, please, the particular significance of paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the notable point with paragraph 17 is the final section of it where it refers to the responsibility over railway security by the Serbian MUP, and this demonstrates to me that there was a connection between -- or there would have been some connection between the use of the railways and the Serbian MUP. And I should also add that, along the principles covered earlier regarding the VJ, specifically the very basic principle that a commander has to know what's going on within his area of responsibility, I would expect that the VJ would also know what use is being made of the railway system during a state of emergency or state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move on to page 22 of the same sector, where you're dealing with the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija. At paragraph 44, it may now be page 23, you touch on an order of the 15th of May, 1998. Its significance, please?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That order provided the mandate at that time for the ministry staff in Kosovo, which I had said earlier had been commanded by General Lukic from that time through the state of war in 1999. And the role from the official mandate is clearly that the MUP staff for Kosovo had responsibility for coordinating the actions of the police activities being run by the SUPs. There's more -- more to the mandate than that, but that's the basis of the mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we move on to page 25, possibly 26, in the subparagraphs of paragraph 47, you're dealing with reporting procedures, and you deal with them extensively. So I just want your comment or focus on subparagraph 5 of paragraph 47.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 5, which comes from instructions on reporting procedures within the MUP, demonstrates to me that there was some form of redundancy built into the MUP system of command and specifically into the system of reporting. Specifically, the SUPs in Kosovo were required to report on their activities to both the ministry in Belgrade and to the MUP staff in Kosovo, and should there have been any block at the level of the ministry staff in Kosovo, the reports would nevertheless have still been sent to the ministry staff in Belgrade. But I should add that I've seen nothing to support any allegation that there was a block at the level of the ministry staff in Kosovo. In fact, I've seen documentation to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally so far as this sector is concerned, at page 37, or it may now be 38, paragraph 67 comes immediately under the heading "Rules Establishing the Internal Organisation of the Ministry of the Interior." Within paragraph 67, you deal with an inspectorate. We can see it at the first subparagraph and within the middle of the second and the third. Can you just highlight for us the particular powers and significance to you of the inspectorate, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This MUP inspectorate, the description provided suggests a form of independent oversight within the MUP itself, and of particular interest is shown in the last paragraph of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be over the page. It's the paragraph beginning: "It shall study instances..." correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The part of that paragraph in which you -- to which you draw your attention.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fourth line in that paragraph, beginning with: "It shall monitor media reports on abuses..." to me, highlights the fact that there was a responsibility to respond to such reports, to media reports on such abuses taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, in all these sectors there's a great deal more detail than the few points that we're taking you to, but it's all been available for reading in a document that has, indeed, I think been filed publicly. So we turn to sector C, please. Here you have the conclusion at page 13 but a summary at page 1. We're going to be troubling the Chamber with some four -- no, five or six references here. Can you give us, in a couple of sentences, what your conclusions were in relation to "The Local Defence Concept in Kosovo," the title of this sector?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The local defence concept was a concept that ensured that, in addition to the regular VJ combat units and military territorial units operating in a combat role under the regular VJ, there were provisions for - and these provisions were implemented for - the establishment of defence forces at the local level, within towns and villages in Kosovo. These defence forces at the local level were set up as early as 1998. And during the setting up of these units, there was a programme for arming the units and arming civilians connected with the local defence concept, and that arming programme was a federal programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We read on page 13, or it may be 14, paragraph 39, you use the word "saturated," saying that the local defence concept ensured that Blank page inserted to make pagination between French and English transcript correspond 24 25 Kosovo was saturated with armed organisations. In the same paragraph, you conclude that, "The concept involved brought FRY and Serb forces together in composite units acting, ultimately, on the authority of the president." "Saturated"?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That term is intended to emphasise that not only in Kosovo was defence a responsibility of the regular army, the VJ, and to a large extent also the combat units of the MUP, but there was also, complementing that and taking away some of the load of defending towns and villages, a well-organised system of local defence, and that system was integrated within the federal system of command which I've described elsewhere in the documentation and alluded to at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps one other aspect of your conclusions, before we look at a couple of pages, can be found in paragraph 41. As to the possibility of illegal armed groups acting without official sanction, what did your analysis of the local defence concept in Kosovo reveal?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In analysing the documentation on local defence, it was clear to me that there was a full intention of integrating within a formal system of command all armed groups, and that included armed civilians, armed civilian defence units, and reserve elements of the police. There was no evidence to suggest -- that I was aware of to suggest that any groups were operating outside of official chains of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Looking at a few references in sector C in a little more detail, and I'm grateful to the usher for putting page 13 on the overhead projector, which helped. If we can now go to page 4 and paragraph 13 in the section of this part headed "Civilian Protection and Civilian Defence Units." You draw our attention in paragraph 13 to Civil Defence Units. Your comment, please?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My comment on this is simply that there were provisions in federal legislation for the formation of armed groups engaged in local defence capacities. And those groups could have some -- according to the legislation, could be commanded at times by VJ officers, as it says, by VJ officer commanding a battalion or higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can turn over to section 5 of this part or of this section, rather. Paragraph 27, which is probably on page 9. It may start on page 8. Paragraph 27, please. And I think there's an exhibit we can look at it, please. Courtesy copies coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, some of these exhibits in the tabbed exhibits of the witness's exhibits have also been produced by other witnesses. Not very many, but some. It may help to have a cross-reference, and we'll provide a complete cross-reference in due course. This exhibit was produced as Exhibit 205 -- 245, I beg your pardon, through a witness called Shukri. It's a large exhibit. There are just courtesy copies available. And if one could be provided to the witness for his comment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all paragraph 27, and then the exhibit, Mr. Coo.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 27 refers to an extract from an instruction issued in 1998 by an organisation known as the Joint Command for Kosovo. The Joint Command was a body tasked with coordinating operations and coordinating events in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999. The instruction it issued in July 1998 formed the basis of the organisation of local defence -- formalised the organisation of local defence as it existed in Kosovo. And that organisation was centred at the municipality level around municipal defence staffs which representation on the municipal defence staffs included municipal politicians, the VJ, military territorial units, the MUP, and civilian defence units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The exhibit we're looking at, which is tab 23, alternatively Exhibit 245, on the overhead projector, please. This is a document dated the 28th of July, 1990 query 8, it would appear, of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Ministry of Defence, Pristina defence administration to defence departments and sections, subject: "Instructions for the Defence of Inhabited Areas." Your comment on the document, Mr. Coo, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document issued by the federal body responsible for administering and coordinating civilian defence. It's Kosovo headquarters reacting to the instructions issued by the Joint Command on the organisation of local defence, or what it calls defence of inhabited areas. And this document from the federal civilian defence headquarters instructs its sub-units to respond and act in accordance with the Joint Command instruction. The Joint Command instruction is attached, and the 11 pages, I think it is, of the Joint Command instruction lay out in a quite detailed fashion how local defence is going to be set up at the municipality level. And the details of those 11 pages include the establishment of what they call reserve task forces of the MUP. And those reserve task forces of the MUP it describes as being comprised of military territorial units, civilian defence units, and units tasked with reporting on activities going on in Kosovo. These are all captured by the reserve task forces of the MUP. Command responsibility for -- for the activities of these reserve task forces of the MUP rests with a MUP officer. The headquarters from which that MUP officer commands these local defence forces are described as municipal defence staffs. And as I mentioned, these staffs include representatives from the politicians at the municipal level, the military territorial representative in the municipality, the VJ, and civilian defence units, along with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we turn over, in your report, to page 11 -- there is one other document we may look at at this stage. Paragraph 33, I suspect still on page 11. And then we'll look at a document as well, or the document indeed that's referred to. Your general comment, first, on paragraph 33 and then we'll provide an exhibit. Tab 67 of part I, a document also admitted through Shukri. The witness had given Exhibit number 248.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petar Ilic was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just wait for the distribution, I think, of the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Leave it with your report until such time as you want to put the exhibit on the projector. Tell us, please, about Petar Ilic.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 33, the reference to Petar Ilic, he was the head of that federal Ministry of Defence headquarters charged with responsibility for civilian defence units in Kosovo and Civilian Protection Units. In this document, an extract of which is provided in paragraph 33, and if we go to the exhibit itself, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It would be the second page of the exhibit and the first substantial paragraph, I think.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second page of the exhibit. At the top of the exhibit, we see that Petar Ilic is addressing his superior in the federal Ministry of Defence, who at that time was General Farkas. In the document, Petar Ilic is responding or appears to be responding to direction that he's received that -- direction concerning the arming of units that fall within the responsibility of that federal Ministry of Defence body, the area organ or Pristina defence administration. The second paragraph, after the word "Belgrade" in the exhibit, beginning with: "In our communication..." --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And incidentally, we must observe that the translation of the exhibit is different from the -- just different slightly in form from the earlier translation in your report, so we'll read from the exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That paragraph beginning: "In our communication..." and strictly confidential number 80-10/3, that's referring to the message member of their communication, "... we request that the command of the 3rd Army secure for us arms and ammunition for all units that are being formed and developed by departments and sections on the territory of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija." And it's clear from this paragraph that the Pristina defence Blank page inserted to make pagination between French and English transcript correspond 24 25 administration has requested from the VJ 3rd Army the issue of weapons, and a large number of weapons, for its civilian defence units. And interestingly too, it's also requested weapons for civilian protection units. The definition of civilian protection units provided in the law on defence makes no suggestion of them being armed. Civilian defence units, in contrast, are defined as being armed units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. That concludes, I think, the matters of detail we wanted to take you through for sector C. So if we go to D, coming towards the end of the first report. D is only in five pages and it has conclusions on page 5 of 5 which the usher might be good enough to lay on the overhead projector, this section being headed "Supreme Command and Joint Command." Rather simply than reading out the conclusions, which can be viewed by those looking at the overhead projector or the screens, in your own words, please, Mr. Coo -- not in your own words but in today's language, as it were, other than the language of your report, what were your conclusions and summary?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conclusions, Your Honours, were that there was an entity known as the Supreme Command at the very top of the chain of command, responsible for the activities of armed organisations and other organisations in Kosovo, in 1999 in particular, during the state of war declared on the 24th of March. The documentation shows the Supreme Command to have consisted of at least the General Staff of the VJ. That is the highest level of command, of military command, headed by General Ojdanic. Above him, within the Supreme Command again, was the civilian command, and at the very top, and at the very top of the whole Supreme Command was the FRY president. Another body which in essence mirrored the structure of the Supreme Command but at a more local level within Kosovo was an entity known as the Joint Command for Kosovo. Again, that was headed by a politician, and its responsibility covered the coordination of the activities of the VJ and the MUP and, in general, armed organisations in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I need ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, in paragraph 13, you mention some challenges to the legality of the Supreme Command. Could you clarify that a little further.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In preparing this report, I came across media articles reflecting the opinions of, among others, General Perisic, who was the former chief of the General Staff and who had been replaced in November 1998. I don't recall exactly, but either during or after the 1999 war, he commented publicly that the Joint Command -- excuse me, that the Supreme Command or specifically that the title "Supreme Commander" was an illegal title. I've seen nothing in the documentation, specifically in FRY legislation, that describes the Supreme Command and the title "Supreme Commander." But on the other hand, all of the orders issued during the state of war, from what I saw as the top level of military or command of the armed forces, was coming from and had the title block "Supreme Command." Those documents and other documents and press statements provided by the 3rd Army commander, General Pavkovic, after the war, which I've provided in the report, all state and make reference to the Supreme Command Staff being the command -- being the VJ General Staff, the Supreme Commander being the FRY president, specifically Mr. Milosevic, and the Supreme Command itself being the body charged with the top level of command responsibility for armed organisations. So nothing supported any arguments put forth by the likes of General Perisic, other than the fact that I didn't come across any legislation that specifically identified a Supreme Commander or Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. As we move beyond section D, there are recognition guides for uniforms, weapons, vehicles, and patches provided. Your Honours, I'm not going to take time with those, they're available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do they relate to the various documents that we've exhibited --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- in Exhibit 17, 18, and 20? Because if so, we should at least see that they do fit in. Well, the photographs refer to K2766. That is our Exhibit 18, I think. Yes. The weapons, 2767, which should be our Exhibit 17. No. Well, we've done the uniforms. Let's move on to the vehicles then. I'm going to do the vehicles next.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The vehicles is 2765.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, 2765, Exhibit 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And finally, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Patches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The patches, which I don't know if we've had exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The patches, I think, have not been -- the patches, I think, have not been exhibited, Your Honour. Do you have them in your copies of the reports? If not, there are copies available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I don't think we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The patches coming up. We're somewhat limited in the number of coloured ones available. Perhaps they should be separately exhibited, Your Honour, not having had a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 322.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Reverting to the weapons, I am told - I should have alerted you at the time - it's Exhibit 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Exhibit, Appendix E, refers to a number of photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, if those haven't been made available to the Judges immediately, I will deal with it after the break and press on with Part II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We do have the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You do have the photographs. Then it's only comment on page -- paragraph 9 that I want the witness to deal with it. There's a photograph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we don't have those photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll come back to that after the break. It won't take me a minute to deal with it then. Better then rather than wasting time now -- taking time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, we'll move on, please, with the reservation about the photographs, to your second report. Bearing in mind the ruling yesterday, can you just summarise the additional work that you did for the second report, the materials you had, and then very briefly the sorts of conclusions you reached, although we'll go through the sections of the parts of the report individually, highlighting particular points. So the task, the materials, and the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Part II of the report is intended to demonstrate whether or not the armed organisations and the command structures were implementing or exercising the doctrine and the regulations provided in Part I.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your conclusions, in short order.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Overall, I had to conclude that the armed organisations and their means of command were exercising to some extent the doctrine and the regulations and, additionally, that there was certainly recognition of what the doctrine and the regulations stated. Furthermore, the structures described in Part I, the local defence and the military and MUP structures, were shown to have been used in Kosovo in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Part A of your second report is in 13 pages or thereabouts. If the usher could have a copy of that available. As it's the amended version, we'll see from time to time amendments, all of which are reflected in the text, whereby paragraphs have been renumbered, and I'd Blank page inserted to make pagination between French and English transcript correspond 24 25 ask you, please, to go straight away within the section "Arming and disarming of Kosovars," to page 12, paragraph 26 that was formerly paragraph 27 before amendment. And here's a document we're going to look at. Tell us about this, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, issued in May 1991, again by that federal Ministry of Defence organ for the civilian defence structures in Kosovo, here in 1998 was issuing a document which to me suggested that not only were the official standing armed organisations being issued arms but also civilians, and primarily ethnic Serb and Montenegrin civilians, were being issued weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A courtesy copy is coming for a document that's within -- this is also within Part I, this exhibit. Yes, I think it's in Part I at tab 21 that you referred to in this second report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this one has not been previously exhibited. The original is, accordingly, available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This document can, as I understand it, stay within the tab number. This is the purpose; it's whichever Part I is, tab 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct. Can we look at it on the overhead projector. As I say, the original is available, if sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So from the same Petar Ilic, in the document dated the 21st of May, 1998, the parts of it on which you place reliance, please, Mr. Coo.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the subtitle "Order" within page 1 of that document, paragraph 1, "Chiefs of departments and heads of sections ..." this is a reference to chiefs of civilian defence departments and their sub-units, known as sections. It requires those heads, those chiefs, to liaise with municipal leaders, politicians, and this is for the purpose of the arming of parts of the population. And it goes on to say, where it begins: "Take care to ensure that those whose wartime duty station is in the units of the VJ..." and so on, the listing of those units, VJ, military, territorial, and MUP, federal Ministry of -- on to page 2 -- federal Ministry of Defence, that list covers, to my awareness, all armed -- all formal official armed organisations. This order addresses the army of civilians outside that list of official armed organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That is all I think we desire to focus on in this first part of your report. And we come to part B, Command and Control, which is in 21 pages, and you will recall that there had been several deletions from this pursuant to the Court's decision. It's a section that has conclusions at page 20, or possibly now 21. There is one document we're going to look at in a couple of seconds, but the conclusions of paragraph 32 and 33 on the overhead projector, your conclusions modulated by the rulings of the Court, please, as to this sector of your report.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my assessment, the removal of those parts of the report would not affect the conclusions in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So your conclusions were?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I concluded that there was a well-structured system of commanding the armed organisations, all armed organisations, in Kosovo. That structure had its basis in the federal regulations and the VJ and MUP internal regulations which I covered in Part I of the report. The issue of whether or not the VJ was subordinated to the MUP in accordance with an article from the law on defence, specifically Article 17, is addressed. Any of the controversy surrounding that issue of subordination was essentially internal to the MUP and the VJ and came out in public debate between commanders of the MUP and the VJ. But for our purposes, the means of commanding those organisations existed and reflected the official doctrinal means of command. And furthermore, the conduct of joint operations, in particular the conduct of joint operations by the VJ and the MUP, combat operations, had a system, and again it was a system based in the doctrine and the laws and the regulations, a system of command. And that system brought in the Joint Command and the chains of command of the VJ and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In paragraph 32 and on the fifth line shown on the screen, you used the word "FRY president, as head of the VJ is likely ... therefore, to have had authority over the Serbian MUP." Can you explain your use of the word "likely" and also whether there was any evidence to the contrary effect.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The use of the word "likely" is -- reflects the fact that I have not seen a single document which states specifically -- or which is signed specifically by the FRY president giving orders directly to the MUP, but all of the documentation, and there was a vast amount of it and much of it what I would consider independent, all led to the assessment that clearly the chain of command which the MUP fell into could be traced back to the office of the FRY president. And the tracing back goes either through the VJ or through the Joint Command. In fact, the tracing back would have to go through both chains in some way, but in very simple terms, all of the documentation shows that you can trace back MUP operations to the office of the federal president.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you conclude your paragraph 32 with the sentences dealing with the Joint Command and the joint operations and your conclusion that "... regular liaison all point to both military and MUP being under the effective control of a single body fulfilling the intentions of a common plan. The scope of what was happening in the FRY and Serbia make the origin of that control and common plan in the office of the FRY president." Now, is that an opinion of yours expressed on the materials available to you or is that anything different?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is primarily a conclusion reached from a review of documentation. It's not -- it doesn't have a great deal of basis in military expert opinion. Its basis is in the -- the expertise came through the review of military related documentation, and this is a logical conclusion, in my assessment, from the documentation I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Rather than a particular military expert?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two documents to look at in this sector. I observe the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It will be convenient to deal with them after the adjournment. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Within section B, Command and Control of your Part II report, at page 12 paragraph 15, there is one exhibit to look at. The exhibit is tab 19 of Part II - courtesy copies coming up - the first sheet of which is the declaration by the deputy chief of investigations, and so the document itself starts on the second sheet, page number 1. Paragraph 15 of your report, then, first, says, and it's a short passage that I can read, I'm just waiting for the usher who has been busy with lots of things. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 15 of part B. I'll read it out while it's being found. No, that's not the right one. It's part B, page 12 of the second report. Don't fuss. Don't worry. Take your time. I'll read it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You said this, Mr. Coo: "The Joint Command for Kosovo coordinated operations by armed organisations in Kosovo (military, MUP, local defence). Joint Command daily situation reports show this through mention of proposed activities for the military and the MUP."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Usher, don't worry about this extract for the time being. It's not your fault; mine for not giving you earlier notice. But if we can just put the exhibit on and then Mr. Coo can comment on that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, perhaps you'll deal with the exhibit and I can alert the usher to the fact that we're going to move to part C, and the first reference will be page 17 of part C. No hurry. Plenty of time. Mr. Coo, tell us about this exhibit, please, and its significance.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first page of the exhibit, or the one after the Blank page inserted to make pagination between French and English transcript correspond 24 25 declaration, which -- provides -- has the title Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, which is the Joint Command I alluded to earlier responsible for coordinating armed organisations in Kosovo. It's titled an operations report which simply, to me, means that it's a report covering operations conducted by the -- or to be conducted by the armed organisations. It begins with and it's structured in accordance with military documents that are familiar to me from my own military experience and military documents that I also came across issued by the VJ because of the fact that it begins with coverage of the -- what we term the enemy, the enemy situation. Here it's called the intelligence and security situation because it's -- probably because it covers slightly broader issues than merely the situation concerning the enemy. It then goes on in the following pages to cover activities of the units of the Yugoslav army and the MUP. This is broken down into sections, one on page 3 which is an overview of, in my assessment, it's an overview of what activities VJ and MUP units have been engaged in. The next subsection, on page 6 of the exhibit, is titled "Proposal for further engagement," and that, to me, shows some responsibility on the part of the Joint Command, certainly involvement of the Joint Command in what the units of the VJ and the MUP are doing in Kosovo. And I think that's the extent of my assessments on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can see throughout these detailed paragraphs references to very substantial number of villages and towns, many of which names may now be familiar to the Chamber. Very well. Let's move from section B to section C, which is "Tactics." It's 14 pages only. It has no paragraph at the front or back headed "Conclusion." We're going to take the Chamber to one page only, bearing in mind the deletions that have also been made from this sector - one deletion - can you tell us, please, what your overall conclusions, if any, on tactics were.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I concluded that the -- through 1998 and 1999, fairly routine use was made of tactics common --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have been following all of this very attentively, everything that the witness has been saying, and as amicus curiae, I think it is my duty to say that the decision of the Court was very clear, that the witness cannot give conclusions of his own. Therefore, I think that I have to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We in fact went through the report and deleted those parts which we felt the witness could not give evidence on, and therefore, they have been excluded. But he is entitled to give evidence on the other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do agree, but Mr. Nice keeps insisting on new conclusions and new comments. That's why I'm saying this. I know what your decision was, and I understand that, but Mr. Nice keeps insisting on new conclusions with regard to other documents, and they are self-explanatory, on the one hand, and on the other hand, it will be for you to assess them at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. I'm sure Mr. Nice will stay within the report and within the spirit of our ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, I return to the question I asked you on tactics, please. You have told us so far through 1998 and 1999 fairly routine use was made of particulars, and then Mr. Tapuskovic addressed us.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The -- to summarise the content of part C and specifically the documentation on which I relied to compile part C, it was apparent to me that the VJ and the MUP were operating together on joint operations, using tactics that appeared to be consistent through 1998 and 1999. And in general terms, the common roles of the VJ and the MUP were that the VJ provided the heavy weapons support to combat operations while the MUP special units, when engaged in joint operations with the VJ, operated as much like an infantry unit and were responsible for moving on to objectives on foot, and those objectives might be villages or KLA strongholds, KLA locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Turning to "Joint Operations," which starts on page 6 of part C and continues through, amongst others, to paragraph 10 on page 7 -- it may be page 8, but I think it's probably still page 7. Paragraph 10, part C. Mr. Coo, you pick out two operational reports, one from 1998 and one from 1999, that illustrate the conduct of joint VJ/MUP operations, and, as you suggest, do much to corroborate numerous other reports suggesting standard practices, because they were used on different operations conducted weeks or months apart. Now, both these reports were issued by Battle Group 4, the 125th VJ Motorised Infantry Brigade, and perhaps you'd like to comment on them. Is the first one the one we've looked at already? The first one coming up, please. Volume I, tab 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Usher, if you'd be so good, please. I will help the Chamber, because I'm sure I can finish within half of this session. There are about, I think, about three more, four more exhibits within the report and half a dozen references. We must go back to the first report. There is then additional documents, about six, that have only recently been available and have been served on the accused. I think we're in good shape to finish about halfway through this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Part I, tab 66, dated the 25th of September, 1998, from command combat group 4, or command group 4, to command of the 125th Motorised Brigade. Draw to our attention what supports your conclusions so far.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to explain some of the background to this document, a battle group or combat group is a formation formed from the components of a brigade, and it's slightly larger than a military company in size and includes a mix of unit types and weapons. And battle groups, from the documentation, were a standard way or a standard formation used by the VJ in combat operations. This document is a report from one such battle group. It's a battle group formed from the 125th Motorised Brigade of the VJ, and that brigade was one of the combat brigades of the Pristina Corps subordinate to 3rd Army. This report from September 1998, is a review of an operation conducted by that Battle Group 4, and the review is -- to me, is being provided for the Battle Group 4's superior command, the command of the 125th Brigade. And in the review, they provide an overview of the operation that they conducted. The information that I focused on in this report concerned the types of weapons, the composition of the battle group, and in particular the fact that the battle group had made reference to conducting the operation with -- jointly with a unit of the MUP, and that MUP unit was -- is known as a PJP unit, which is, as mentioned earlier, one of the MUP's special units, heavily armed units designed for combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if we then turn to the second report, the one in early 1999, February of 1999, which is tab 2 of Part II, which is also Exhibit 94, and tab 47 of that exhibit. Mr. Coo, again, and as shortly as you can, draw the identifying -- I beg your pardon, the significant points and perhaps the similar points from this document that you focused your attention on.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, this is a document from that same battle group of that same VJ brigade months later, showing that the battle group was still engaged in -- or again engaged in combat operations, and those combat operations were taking place jointly with units of the MUP, specifically the PJP. One of the details of this order, attack order, is worth noting, in my opinion, is just how detailed the order is. It's a relatively low-level unit, a combat group or battle group, and this is -- this order provides quite an extensive description of the attack which is to take place, and it shows how much planning has to go into organising and Blank page inserted to make pagination between French and English transcript correspond 24 25 conducting an attack, the authority for which would come from more senior commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber can read the detail themselves on several pages. There's no particular item of it, it's the generality of the detail that you rely on, I think.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We turn then from part C to part D, which is in 13 pages, 13, possibly 14 by now. Thirteen, I think. It's headed "Operations in Kosovo." It has no expressed conclusion. Can you summarise the effect of this part of your report? And we'll take the Chamber to two passages or perhaps one passage only.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This section of the report used various sources to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Some of which, of course, have now been deleted, and you've got to take account of that.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Concerning the deleted sections, in my assessment, they don't affect the overall scope of part D. They -- they were corroboration of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Say no more about them, providing they don't assess the conclusion. Your conclusions or the summary of the effect of this part being what, Mr. Coo, please?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a review of various sources, documentary sources, to show the scale of operations being conducted by armed operations in Kosovo during the period of interest in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go, then, to one page, page 4, paragraph 2. It runs into page 5. We don't need to look at an exhibit. You quote from something here, and indeed it's General Pavkovic's letter of the 23rd of July to his superiors when commanding the Pristina Corps. Your comment, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is General Pavkovic in his previous appointment as commander of the Pristina Corps, prior to commanding the 3rd Army. The letter is, to me, a demonstration of his disagreement with the way in which the conflict in Kosovo, or specifically the VJ's role in that conflict, was going. And it shows the opinions of a VJ commander in a very key position during 1999. And one of the items in the letter and in the extract provided in paragraph 2 states that -- or makes reference to the arming of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It says in terms, "Despite the arming of the population, that factor in the system against terrorist struggle has not been included."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just assess from that that the population has been armed, and that is what I covered earlier, the arming of civilian defence units and the civilians themselves, provided for in other documentation, and it that General Pavkovic is -- doesn't feel that this has been -- the employment of these armed civilians has not been fully implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Probably obvious but it perhaps should be stated that your observation at the conclusion of the quotation about the reference to loss of Kosovo and genocide of Serbs is not a military expert conclusion, it's a general conclusion that anybody might or might not adopt, depending on their judgement.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So we can move, then, to section E, headed "Crime Site Linkage," being on merely seven sides. Having neither express preamble or concluding conclusions, the purpose and effect of this sector -- section of your report, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the scope of this section is to cover how I as a military analyst and also with my -- with consideration of the documentation that I reviewed and covered in other sections, how I would examine and how I did examine some of the documentation related to either crime sites or attacks in general conducted by armed organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You draw to our attention your paragraph 4 on the foot of page 1 and over to page 2, and you say this: "When a distinction between military and MUP cannot be made easily, it is still possible to demonstrate that the attacking organisation was, nevertheless, an organised armed group, and the possibility that it was a rogue or a regular or paramilitary group operating outside an official chain of command or outside the awareness of such a chain of command can be countered using the following reasoning..." bearing in mind the decision of the Chamber about testimony on which they have to make judgements generally applied, your remaining comment for this paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- this paragraph reflects the other sections of the report in which I assess that, or I show and documentation shows to me, the scope of the arming of groups and organisations in Kosovo, how widespread that was. It's also how I, as a military analyst, would assess reports concerning the identity of groups engaged in operations, whether those operations concerned one of our indictment sites or any other -- or attacks in general. And there's various indicators or various types of information that I would use in making such assessments. And some of this includes the description of uniforms, and I would rely on those descriptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. If we turn over, please, to page 4, you identify the Prizren municipality. And there's an extract from the report. I may not be able to show it on the overhead projector, but the citation is given at footnote 4. You have it. It's coming up your way. Thank you very much. And it's actually from volume I of the exhibits, tab 34, which should be cross-referenced to its other label, which is Exhibit 281. Now, so far as this document is concerned, Mr. Coo, if you have it before you, its significance is what and then take us to the part of the report if you can find it immediately.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report from the -- the MUP headquarters, the MUP staff for Kosovo charged with coordinating MUP operations in Kosovo. It shows, among other things, in the header that the MUP staff is reporting to the ministry in Belgrade. And this is during the state of war and specifically 27 March 1999. The section of interest in Part II E of my report, the passage concerning an attack by the KLA in -- or by terrorists, as mentioned in the report, on the 25th of March in the Prizren municipality shows to me that the VJ and the MUP at that time were engaged in an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's on page 4 of the exhibit. Just throw it up on the screen. And it's in the middle of that page. The paragraph reading: "In a terrorist attack carried out on the 25th of March ..." Carry on, please, Mr. Coo.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This passage simply makes reference to members of both the MUP and the VJ being injured in attack in that municipality on that day. And from that, I assess that an operation was being conducted, or at least the VJ and the MUP were in the -- in that -- in those areas on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For reasons of time, if we stay on your report, on page 4, and look at Racak on which we've seen a great deal of -- in respect of which we've had a great deal of evidence, you cite a telegram sent by the SUP of Orahovac, reporting details of the incident to the ministry in Belgrade on the 15th of January. Just check that that's on the screen. And then it goes over onto the following page, the citation of the quotation, page 5. "Starting at 0300 hours on the 15th of January, measures were taken to seal off the village of Racak."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm going to interrupt you just to clarify this. I think this is a report which we've already had exhibited, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may well be. I'll get the number for it, if we can find it. It's K1599 but I'm afraid I don't have the exhibit number immediately. I will obtain it, if so, and provide it. May I just continue briefly with the quotation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You also draw to our attention five lines down, the indented passage: "At 630, the village was completely encircled while a part of the PJP, special police units, was advancing right at the entrance into the village." In the concluding subparagraph: "No civilians were hurt during the execution of the operation." Significance of that, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This simply shows that the PJP, MUP unit, was involved in the Blank page inserted to make pagination between French and English transcript correspond 24 25 attack on Racak on the 15th of January, and this is the MUP, or the SUP in that area reporting to its superiors on that action.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just turning up the exhibit number, if we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's in a binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll find it. Can I come back to it and give you the reference in a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On page 7 of this part of your report, Mr. Coo, right at the conclusion in respect of Izbica, you make reference to the Vojska 2001, and to an investigation carried out by the VJ itself in respect of Izbica. And in that book, is there a quotation to the effect that on the basis of the order of the investigating judge in Kosovo Mitrovica, the same team carried out an external examination and identification of 101 bodies in the village of Izbica, Srbica municipality?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a reference to such an examination conducted by the VJ in 1999 during the state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Still tracking that other exhibit, Your Honour. May I come back to it? I've marked the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, apart from annexes, there's part F of your report on "Discipline." It's in nine pages. It has no particular expressed conclusion. In summary, though, Mr. Coo.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
