utterances.text: In Part I, I set out to show from the documentation how -- what the disciplinary procedures and how the disciplinary system in the armed organisations was supposed to work, was set up, the regulatory basis for it. In this section of Part II, I -- I set out to show from the documentation how the disciplinary system was actually implemented in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it possible to say anything in summary as to how it was implemented in practice or are we better off just reading the seven pages and looking at two items of them now?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honours, the documentation showed a recognition on the part of the armed organisations of the formal systems of discipline. The exercise of those systems is a different question and addressed in this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So if we can look first at page 2, paragraph 5. And of course having in mind that the operation of the disciplinary system is largely a matter of fact for the Chamber, save insofar as it might be supported positively or negatively by documentation at the time. We find you in paragraph 5 saying this: "According to all information reviewed in the process of compiling this report, there was in 1999 the required structures and measures for an effective system of discipline over armed organisations of the FRY and Serbia. Commanders at all levels would have been fully aware of the requirements for maintaining discipline. The mere issuance of instructions and orders is insufficient to meet the responsibility which commanders have for discipline." And you then go on. Perhaps you will conclude this paragraph in your own words, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Specifically, Your Honours, the -- in the middle of that paragraph, beginning with, "... the mere issuance of instructions is insufficient..." this refers back to Part I where the disciplinary regulations are covered in detail for both the MUP and the VJ. And part of those regulations concerns command responsibility. One extract in particular highlights the responsibility of commanders for taking action in the event of violations of the laws of war or humanitarian law or violations of internal regulations related to discipline. In Kosovo, with the indictment in mind, I reviewed the documentation available to me on the exercise of disciplinary measures and what that documentation showed and the documentation available to me showed was that some disciplinary measures were taken, and these are provided in the report. No disciplinary measures, to my awareness, were taken concerning command responsibility, and some of the basis for this assessment on my part was the fact that all of the -- if not all, most of the commanders in key positions, brigade commanders, corps commander, and higher, and equivalents in the MUP were either promoted or retained -- and/or retained. And similarly, units that they commanded, some of the documentation shows those units receiving commendations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we go on, please, to page 7 of this sector, "Clearing Up the Battlefield." This is something that has been touched on quite a lot in evidence one way and another. Just without going through the details, summarise the effect of the regulations you've considered.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The regulations and the orders issued concerning clearing up the battlefield suggests to me that they had well-established procedures, and they at least made an effort to exercise those procedures concerning the clearing up of, amongst other things, dead bodies in Kosovo. And this was -- made it very apparent that it's not part of the doctrine that bodies should merely be left lying around on the battlefield. On the contrary, there's a requirement in cleaning up the battlefield, or clearing up the battlefield, that any bodies that they do come across where there's suspicion of criminal wrongdoing, that there's an obligation on the part of the VJ and other organisations to conduct investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your annexes to this report start immediately after page 9. We can deal with them very briefly. The first annex is simply key personnel and an annex of reference. These aren't, I think, page numbered. I only have Registry pages to go on, and they may be different from those in the version being considered by the Chamber. So we then go to annex 2, which I have on Registry page 13787. Just explain annex 2 to us. It begins with Bajgora, Donji Ratis, Gornji Ratis and so on.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contents of annex 2 are extracts from the OSCE's daily reporting on events in Kosovo and their reporting concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's only very lightly headed so it's hard to find. It comes on the page immediately following footnote 149.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have it now. Yes. This is the document and we have the exhibit number so it can be referred to. It's Exhibit 321, the Blue Book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Annex 3, which starts at what I have as -- well, it's just called Part II, annex 3, pages 1 of 4 is VJ Activity. Could you explain that, if you will, for us, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Annex 3 makes use of various documents available to me which show operations conducted by the VJ during the state of war in 1999. The -- I should stress that this would not -- would most likely not be an exhaustive list of where the VJ was operating and what it was doing on a day-to-day basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that's been finally reflected in a map. I'm not going to trouble the Court with it. You can see it there, it's at the end of the document. Returning to the question of the exhibit, Your Honour, it may be that the item referred to is similar to but in fact different from an earlier document. I'm grateful to Ms. Graham and, I think, to the registry for teasing this out. I'm not sure exactly -- and I think the exhibit concerned is 211, one of the documents presented through General Drewienkiewciz. You will see this. It is, in any event, tab -- it's tab 27 of volume II's exhibits. The witness has already dealt with the extract on page 5 of part E of the second report, and one can see it there on that page. That concludes all I want to ask, if that's convenient, about the second report. There's the photographs to be dealt with and the patches in the first report. If I can take the Chamber back to the first report and to Appendix E. The Chamber will see at Appendix E --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, if you have your first report - that's Part I of the reports - at section E, you provide there a guide to a number of photographs that the Chamber will be able to find and not all of which I'm going to ask you to deal with. But at paragraph 9 on page 2, you speak of Blank page inserted to make pagination between French and English transcript correspond 24 25 one particular photograph which I'd like to put on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where are we going to find those photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They're at tab 79. Interesting though they are, I think time dictates that I should only show the one of maximum relevance at the moment. Place this on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, it's something we've heard about to some degree in evidence, and if you look at the photograph, your comment on it, please. We're focusing not on the individuals but on their shoulders and what's on their shoulders, are we not?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honours. Well, these are members of the MUP, special unit PJP, as identified by the uniforms and patches, but specifically in the report it focuses on the wearing of ribbons, ribbons on the shoulders. And there is documentation and references made to that document to show that this was indeed a practice used, adopted by the MUP. The document is a table for one month in 1999, I think, or perhaps 1998, I can't recall exactly, but nevertheless, a table showing what colour arrangement of ribbons should be worn and on which shoulder each day during that month.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Here comes the table, which is volume I of the exhibits, tab 80. If we put the version which is, of course, the English version - the original is available - on the overhead projector. You can see this is detailed instructions to the police for wearing identification bands in May of 1999 with the words "SUP" written in hand on the top on the original. And then day by day, starting on the 1st of May, with the 24 hour appropriate timespan, there is the indication of what is to be worn on the right shoulder epaulette, blue and red, then blue and yellow, and so on. Perhaps we can just look at one more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you do, it may be obvious, but what was the purpose, as you would understand it, of wearing these ribbons and when would they have worn them? Mr. Coo, can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The purpose, in my assessment, was, and it's partially based on what's in the title, where it says "For identification," or they call them identification bands, I think. The purpose is for identification, and the identification to prevent or help prevent MUP from either shooting themselves because they don't recognise their own units in the heat of battle, or to ensure that the KLA, in case -- in the event that they wear police uniforms - and I'm not aware of any documentation showing that - but should the enemy wear uniforms of friendly forces, the friendly forces would at least -- in this case the MUP, would at least have a system for recognising their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just have another look at the photograph briefly. On the overhead projector. You will also see a balaclava there. Do you see a balaclava on the bottom right? Is that a common feature of these photographs or not don't you know?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall whether it's a common feature of the photos provided. It's a common feature of other photographs that I've seen and adopted by special units of both the VJ and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One more photograph: 56304 on page 3 of this section, paragraph 13. Your report suggests that this photograph shows the MUP, probably the PJP, in the field with some variations in dress, the association of all of these men with the MUP coming from the use of the ribbons and the commonness of the MUP blue camouflage uniform with the insignia, probably "Milicija" or "Policija" on the left shoulder, common automatic weapons and MUP vehicles in the background. You're ascribing them to an illegal, as you describe it, paramilitary group coming from what, please, Mr. Coo?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my work, I read a large number of our witness statements --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it may be if that comes from evidence it's not appropriate for you to express that opinion, and I don't press it. The earlier points about the ribbons are matters you are able to express an opinion on.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can add that, in general terms, from reading the media and listening to people without military experience, it is sometimes difficult to identify a military unit. It's sometimes difficult to identify the difference, for them to show that they know the difference between a tank and an armoured personnel carrier, and the use of this photograph is to -- the aim of this photograph is to show that on not all occasions would organised units dress in what might look like clean, parade standard uniforms. These are units engaged in combat; they're dirty. Sometimes military organisations of some countries have insufficient uniforms to properly equip everyone, especially when they've conscripted people, and this may be an occasion where that has taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I pass from your reports to the five documents recently received which will, I think, require separate exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They have been provided to the accused and the amici. They have been translated. It would indeed save time if they could be given a single exhibit number, if that's acceptable to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it in one file or how is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not actually in a file, I think they've just been clipped together at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it may be -- let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It has an index at the front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If we give them one exhibit number, the individual items can be referred to by the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In that case, if those can go -- I have this morning, for reasons of speed, not been pursuing my normal policy of putting B/C/S or Cyrillic B/C/S originals on the overhead projector. I hope that's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 323.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. If we can look at the first of these in English, dated the 7th of April of 1999, from the Supreme Command Staff. And it's, of course, the Supreme Command that may feature on these documents that's of interest. "Military secret, strictly confidential and coded." I think there are a number of paragraphs here that you want to draw to our attention. Can you explain the significance of this order to your general conclusions, please. It comes from General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an order from the Supreme Command Staff, which is covered in detail in my report, and that was the VJ General Staff operating within the Supreme Command, at the top of the chain of command during the state of war. It's concerning the number of volunteers attempting to join the VJ at that time. And this document establishes procedures to -- to be instated, to be practised when accepting volunteers into VJ units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we go to page 2 of the document, the second bullet point as an example, and the third, we see reference to neuropsychiatric examinations and the suitability of volunteers from a security point of view.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those two bullet points show evidence to me of concern about the quality of the volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we go to the third page and to paragraph 10 where the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command prohibits the admission of members of paramilitary groups -- "units, groups, and individuals already present in the zones of responsibility to VJ commands as volunteers without prior completion of procedures regulated by this order." The significance of that, in your judgement?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This to me seems to be an effort on the part of the Supreme Command to ensure that what may be groups operating outside formal chains of command are integrated into formal chains of command in compliance with procedures outlined in this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turn to the next document, number 2 of this exhibit, dated the 9th of April, some days later. Again from the same General Ojdanic to the Blank page inserted to make pagination between French and English transcript correspond 24 25 commander of the 3rd Army personally. And then it's the penultimate paragraph that I think draws your attention and on which I'd like your comment, as on the distribution of the document generally.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- the penultimate paragraph is a demonstration to me of the involvement of the Supreme Commander in the conduct of commanding units subordinate to the Supreme Command Staff and the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because it says: "The report on the proposal for a decision will be submitted on the 11th of April at the Supreme Command Staff in the presence of the Supreme Commander." The proposal itself is the proposal set out for a decision on preventing aggression, with certain variations?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and this is entitled a "Preparatory Order for the Commander of the 3rd Army Personally," and by "personally," I interpret that to mean that they want to limit the distribution of this for operational security reasons to ensure that the -- that a future operation's details aren't compromised. Preparatory orders are issued, exist in the doctrine I reviewed of the VJ, and they also exist in my own military experience where they're called warning orders, and they allow and they're used to provide commanders with opportunities to begin planning procedures before the more detailed order and instruction is issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Document number 3, please. 17th of April. From the Supreme Command Staff to the 3rd Army command, to the commander personally, from General Ojdanic. And underneath that heading, "Link: Kosovo and Metohija Joint Command ..." Significance, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me, the significance of the phrase after the word "link," the reference to the Joint Command for Kosovo order is simply that. It's a reference to the Joint Command having issued an order, and the order implies, to me, executive authority, in this case in relation to combat operations on the part of the Joint Command. It also shows a -- some form of relationship between the Supreme Command, the 3rd Army, and the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Joint Command having, as I think you've explained in your report, a political component to it on your understanding?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Fourth document, 18th of April, again from General Ojdanic. It may be the heading, "Pursuant to the Order of the President" that may be the point of significance on which you would rely.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To me, this is -- this shows the Supreme Command Staff issuing orders on behalf or pursuant to, as it's worded here, an order issued by the federal president. Specifically, it's in relation to Article 17 of the law on defence, which is addressed in my report, and simply covers the provision for subordinating the MUP to the VJ for combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then finally, the fifth document, 10th of May, from General Ojdanic, an order marked "Keep permanently" with an annex which starts on page 3 in the English version. Paragraph 3 of this order directs, "Commanders, unit commanders and other superior officers to undertake necessary measures to prevent violations of the principles, rules, and regulations of the international laws of war..." and goes on to deal with personal responsibility. The significance of this document, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This demonstrates to me the Supreme Command exercising during the state of war what exists, and what's referred to in my report, in documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any other particular points on this last document you want to draw to our attention?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: None other than it's -- I think it's simply an emphasis, a reiteration of the responsibility of commanders and others in the chains of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That concludes all I want to ask this witness. Thank you, Mr. Coo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we're going to take the adjournment now before cross-examination. We will go on with your cross-examination after it. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, Mr. May, what is the total amount of time I will have for cross-examining this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we have to finish tomorrow. We need -- I don't know if the amici have any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We may have, but that may depend on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Obviously not lengthy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are some administrative matters which have to be dealt with tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I would expect that by the time they're ventilated they're likely take an hour and it may be sensible to allow a session, but certainly an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We think three hours should be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coo, you said yesterday that for ten years you worked in the Canadian army on intelligence matters and that during that military career of yours, you obtained the rank of captain; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before joining the Canadian army, did you work on any other matters?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I understand the question, Your Honour. Matters concerning what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you employed in any capacity in any other institution before joining the Canadian military, that is to say, before those ten years you spent in the Canadian army?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I -- before I joined the intelligence branch in 1988, I was at university. During my university years, I was a reservist in the naval reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So practically, you were not employed anywhere, gainfully employed, before you started working for the Canadian army?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my recollection, no, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Which schools have you finished, Mr. Coo?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completed a degree, a Bachelor of Science, at the University of Calgary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was your major, actually? I didn't quite understand this.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I majored in psychology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're a psychologist by training.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't -- I certainly wouldn't describe myself as a psychologist on the basis of having a Bachelor degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you have any other type of education in addition to these studies in psychology? And I said that in terms of your education you were trained to be a psychologist, I did not say that you are a psychologist.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beginning in 1997, when I left the Canadian Forces, I took a number of other university courses. I didn't complete a degree. Those courses were in science.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can I infer on the basis of these answers you've given, quite briefly, that you do not really have any kind of military training or education?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I strongly disagree with that inference. I think my military training is covered in detail in my curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, a part of -- apart from that which is described in your curriculum vitae, could you please explain what is the education you received in the military field? Blank page inserted to make pagination between French and English transcript correspond 24 25

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of my military education was provided for me in the military during my military career, either as a naval reservist or, more importantly, during my career as an intelligence officer. My education in university is not a military education.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I assume that you distinguish between education and experience. You gained some experience by working in the military. However, on the basis of what you have said so far, this was not preceded by any kind of military education, that is to say, you did not complete any kind of military school, military academy, et cetera, something that would be required, for example, for the rank of captain in the army.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Canadian system, we don't have what I think exists in Yugoslavia and that is military schools. We have a Royal Military College which offers university-level degrees. Some officers enter the military through military college. Those officers might take degrees such as engineering or strategic studies or a variety of other degrees found at civilian universities. So there's two entry schemes for officers in the Canadian Forces; one through the military college scheme and another through civilian universities. And I should add, in addition, some officers, at least at the time I joined, did not have to have any university degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But can I understand it this way, Mr. Coo: As far as the military profession is concerned, then, what is required is a military education. As regards a generally usable profession like that of a physician or a lawyer or a psychologist, then they can get a commission in the army because they got a university degree, but they are practising their own profession. For example, somebody who has a degree from the school of medicine can become an officer, but he treats soldiers, but he's not involved in the military line of work. So it's different, isn't it? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would disagree. The Canadian military operates on a system of accepting officers from a variety of educational backgrounds. They don't always require a -- they don't always specify a specific degree. It depends on the component of the military into which you're entering, but, for example, an officer entering the military as an infantry officer does not require a specific degree. An officer entering as a medical officer or an engineering officer does require a specific degree; an engineering or a medical degree. The Canadian Forces makes provisions for not, in some instances, requesting specific degrees. The system has within it a means of providing professional education for its officers, ensuring that they meet the standards, the required standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, during your military career - and you say it lasted ten years - did you command a military unit?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not command a unit that's on the establishment of the Canadian Forces. I had command over a number of soldiers and non-commissioned officers as an officer in a subsection or sub-unit within an establishment unit, or within a number of establishment units. I was not what is officially described as a commanding officer. With the position of commanding officers come a number of capabilities. I can't really phrase it any other way, but commanding officers, for instance, have specific responsibilities towards discipline and specific authorities regarding discipline. I had some but not to the extent that a commanding officer would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Coo. So you reached the rank of captain. You did not command any unit; not a platoon, not a company, not a squad. You do not have a military education. You got a degree in psychology. Is that what we have established so far now that we're dealing with your qualifications?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to disagree quite strongly with that. I did reach the rank of captain. I was not a commanding officer, but I did command units within the Canadian Forces, and I did command soldiers and non-commissioned officers. I was at one point, for example, as provided for in my CV, the officer commanding an intelligence collection and analysis section, a platoon within an intelligence company. I held other similar types of positions. My military education, as I've pointed out, was provided when I was in the military. The skills I gained during my civilian studies were skills that were valued by the Canadian Forces. Otherwise, they wouldn't, I suppose, specify that entering officers have those qualifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now we've come to the point that you say that you commanded a military unit that was not actually a military unit but it was a unit for intelligence collection, if I understood it correctly, right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the example I gave, that's partially correct. It was not a military unit on the establishment of the Canadian Forces books. That unit was, in the example I gave, the First Canadian Division Intelligence Company, and that unit was commanded by a commanding officer, and there's very specific descriptions of what a commanding officer is and his powers of punishment. A commanding officer has more powers of punishment than an officer commanding. I was an officer commanding of a component of that establishment unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You were an officer within that intelligence company. All right, Mr. Coo. We have partly clarified your qualifications. Do you personally think that the experience of an officer who is responsible for a group, a platoon-size group, and who did not complete any military school qualifies you to appear here as a military expert regarding matters concerning an army that had, in wartime, 350.000 persons involved. And also, for all questions of various relations like between the Supreme Command and all types of units - military units, police units, the civilian structure, et cetera - do you believe that this experience of yours qualifies you and that your education qualifies you to appear in this role?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I do for the following reasons, Your Honours: Again, as laid out in my CV, I had -- I filled more positions than the intelligence company. Those positions covered the strategic level of analysis at the national defence headquarters, all the way down to being an intelligence officer in a brigade headquarters, and included in which was experience in a brigade on an operation in Bosnia. The -- both the training provided at the beginning of my career covers strategic analysis. At the time I was in, we were required to understand and we learned about the structures and how forces of the Warsaw Pact were commanded. This training was practised during my career in the various positions I've identified. I was required to provide intelligence support to commanders at various levels, including the deputy chief of the defence staff to whom, in one of my appointments, I briefed on a daily basis about strategic issues. So overall, I think that I've had experience and training in military analysis. I don't pretend to bring with me experience of commanding large formations and, consequently, the report hasn't pretended to introduce any such experience, but I have engaged in analysing the structures and the command of large military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that you studied the organisation of the Warsaw Pact forces. Are you aware of the fact that Yugoslavia was not a member of the Warsaw Pact and that, as concerns organisation of its military, that it did not coincide with the organisation of the forces belonging to the Warsaw Pact?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that the former Yugoslavia was not a Warsaw Pact country. It was not a military that I studied in detail at the time. Some of its organisation conforms to what I remember studying in Warsaw Pact armies. Whether or not it matches precisely the organisation of a Warsaw Pact army is, in my assessment, of no consequence for the report that I wrote. I examined the structure of the Yugoslav army and other armed organisations based on documentation, and any -- any results, any resulting assessments drawn from that documentation clearly has its basis in the documentation. The -- in some cases, supplemented by my military experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You studied documentation, as far as I could see here. Let me start from the constitution of Yugoslavia, the law on defence, the law on the army. You studied orders of commanders in the field and so on. Do you believe that your experience and knowledge makes it possible for you to draw conclusions that have to do with the constitution, laws, orders, command levels, the Supreme Command, corps, brigades, et cetera? Just give me a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- with respect, Your Honours, I can't give a simple yes or no. I can say yes within certain constraints which I adopted and followed in my analysis. I -- I fully admit that I'm no expert on the law. I can interpret the contents of the law on the VJ, for example, and assess its relevance with respect to other documentation that I've seen. I could not engage in a legal debate about the validity of that law with respect to the constitution and FRY legal practices in general, but within the constraints of my analysis, I think I was qualified to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that you're not an expert for law. Do you consider yourself to be an expert for military matters in view of what we have concluded so far, notably for the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again yes, with the explanation that my expertise is very specific and has been outlined. It's in military analysis. I have experiences of operating in militaries and I am familiar with the jargon and the practices, the doctrine of both my own military and a number of other militaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. From what you have been saying, it is my understanding that you base your testimony on this series of documents that you mention. You exhibited some of them here, on the one hand, and on the other hand, on the knowledge that you have concerning certain activities of the military and the police. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contents of my report were almost entirely based on what appeared in the documents mentioned in the report. Some of my military experience was used to interpret -- offer interpretations of the relevance of some of the documentation, but primarily what's in the report is a compilation of military-related documents, the bringing together of those to, in effect, paint a picture of the way things were in the period of interest to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Out of which documents did you gain knowledge about activities? Because you say that from regulations, orders, et cetera, you drew certain knowledge as to how the military functioned. What about the activities? From which documents did you draw your knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: A number of documents, and I think the list is too long to name them all, but they included some that we referred to earlier this morning; the review of operations conducted by a battle group, articles from the VJ's own journal, Vojska magazine, highlighting what various brigades did in Kosovo, comments made by -- in open source materials by various commanders within both the MUP and the VJ, and a number of other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Coo. Let's leave aside now the scarcity or, rather, the constrained nature of such an approach. Even though you had this approach with regard to documents, did you have the same kind of constrained approach when you were looking into the terrorist organisation of the KLA? Did you look at documents that were relevant to their activity, and did you look at information that has to do with their activity, data related to that? Because nowhere here have I seen anything about that.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not asked to examine the operations conducted by the KLA. Furthermore, I was not asked to examine in detail at the crime site activities by armed organisation of the FRY and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On the basis of what did you establish that crimes were committed? On the basis of what are you testifying about crimes?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't established or sought to establish that crimes were committed. It's not a conclusion within the scope of my report or my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But just awhile ago, you mentioned crimes. So you take as your point of departure crimes. On the basis of what did you establish that crimes had been committed?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I haven't tried to establish that. The reference to crimes is a reference to the allegations in the indictment. I have provided some material in the report which is connected to specific indictment sites, but I did not attempt to go beyond the presentation of that material to reach any conclusion about whether or not a crime had been committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since your task was not to compile information or documents about the terrorist forces, is that also in keeping with your own line of work? Namely, yesterday when you were speaking about yourself in response to Mr. Nice's questions as to what your line of work was, you said to collect information and to inform the commander as to what was happening in the field. And then when he asked you whether that pertained to all the enemy forces, your own forces, the allied forces, et cetera, your answer was this information pertains to enemy forces. So you were involved in dealing with enemy forces only. From that position, did you treat the army of Yugoslavia and the police of Yugoslavia as enemy forces? Were you given the assignment to collect information and to analyse documents and the activities of the army of Yugoslavia as an enemy force, as the enemy side? Is that right, Mr. Coo?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't encourage the use of the term "enemy" in this instance because it's a bit of a loaded term, but the process of my analysis of the VJ was the process that I would use to analyse any military force I'd analysed in my military career.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, may I just remind you, yesterday in your explanation, you said that regardless of his employment, et cetera - you quoted a judgement - that an expert can be allowed to testify, and I wrote it down under quotation marks, "if he is an expert in what he is testifying about." On the basis of these elements that we've just heard, is that your conclusion, that the witness is an expert, able to testify about the army of Yugoslavia, the command, organisation, the constitution, et cetera? And then quoting that judgement, is that how you reached your decision that he can testify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The answer is yes. As a military analyst, he is an expert. What weight we give to the evidence, of course, is a matter for us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me start off with this question. It is one that has to do with the beginning of the examination-in-chief pertaining to your second report. As far as I was able to gather, you, in response to a question put to you by Mr. May, said that the procedure and conduct in the army and the armed forces were in keeping with the regulations, the rules and regulations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have to elaborate on the answer. In Part I, I laid out from the documentation what the doctrine, what the regulations were in the VJ and what it was required to operate in compliance with. In Part II, I looked at documentation, some of which related to whether or not they exercised and practised those regulations. Some of the documentation I viewed shows recognition that those regulations existed. For example, the large number of orders issued urging VJ units to comply with the laws of war and humanitarian law, to me, demonstrate recognition of the -- of the legislation and the internal regulations of the VJ which are outlined in Part I. I did not conclude from the documentation reviewed for Part II that the compliance with the doctrine and the legislation and the regulations was either comprehensive or 100 percent or complete. There was just insufficient documentation to reach such a conclusion or assessment. There were elements of recognition on the part of the VJ of their own internal regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right, then. Did you come by any documents or gain any Blank page inserted to make pagination between French and English transcript correspond 24 25 information on the basis of which you were able to conclude that, contrary to those regulations, that something was done illegally, contrary to those regulations, any criminal acts or anything of that nature? And if so, could you indicate those documents to me, please.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any documentation from the VJ, the MUP, or the other organisations relating specifically to the commission of criminal acts other than references to, and these are in Part II of the report on -- section on discipline. There are references to violations of regulations - in some cases the Criminal Code - where they point out that they've conducted investigations and brought disciplinary measures against a number of soldiers. I haven't seen sufficient documentation -- sorry. That's my answer, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As you've already brought that up and as you're here now, you say you saw documents on the basis of which one can -- could establish that precisely in keeping with the regulations of the Yugoslav army, the army and the police prosecuted the perpetrators of criminal acts which were established. However, as far as I recall, in answer to a question put to you, you said that you do not have any information or data about commanders being punished in any way. And my question to you is this: Why should the commanders be punished if their conduct was in keeping and compliance with the rules and regulations and if they brought individuals to accountability, individuals who had perpetrated certain criminal acts? Why should they be then held responsible themselves? And there are many individuals who were brought to task and prosecuted. So why do you think the commanders ought to be punished if they did so in conformity with their duty and the laws governing the army?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's the role of -- or it's certainly not my role to reach conclusions about whether or not the punishment of commanders was sufficient in light of the crimes we allege in the indictment. I merely point out in the report when the crimes in the indictment are considered against the acts of discipline being taken, as I saw in the documentation, I thought it worthwhile to point out that - for the consideration of the Trial Chamber - that the commanders in the VJ and the MUP in the key positions were all either promoted or retained after and during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But what you're saying now is that you're comparing that to the alleged crimes stipulated in the indictment. Now, is it clear to you as an employee of the OTP that what is alleged in the indictment and set forth there can be fabricated, incorrect, or quite simply launched in order to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've been through this with another witness. That's not a matter for the witness. He merely has to go on what's in the document. It's a matter for us to determine whether what you suggest might be true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the witness is drawing conclusions the whole time, although that is your job, or, rather, it ought to be the job of every legal Trial Chamber to draw its own conclusions and not to allow the witness to do that. And the witness is using the allegations made in the false indictment to draw his own conclusions. So the fact of the matter is, I would say, quite clear, and that is why I asked him the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ask him another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When Mr. Nice asked you a question, he mentioned a joint plan. Could you tell us what joint plan this was, what it's all about, and where is it? What document do you -- what document do you in fact talk about when you talk about this joint plan? What is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't remember a joint plan. A joint command there was talk of, but no joint plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a reference. I think it's in section E. I'm not sure it's a concluding section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Refer it to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it is. Mr. Coo will correct me if I'm wrong. I think he probably is referring to what can be found in Part II -- part B of Part II, and the concluding lines of paragraph 32, which I have on page 21. It's not joint, it's "common plan."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: "The scope of what was happening in the FRY and Serbia make the origin of that control and common plan in the office of the FRY president."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, would you explain to me, please, on the basis of which you make that observation about this common plan?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis is in -- again in the documentation I've reviewed and some expert opinion. The -- the documentation from 1998 through 1999 that I reviewed shows the MUP and the VJ operating on a regular basis in combat operations in Kosovo, the number of the units, of such units, the fact that it was the -- at least a corps level responsible for Kosovo engaged in such operations and all of the MUP units in Kosovo, to me, demonstrate the scale of the operations. The scale of the operations, as I've just said, covering all of Kosovo or encompassing all of the units in Kosovo has to, on the principles that I provide in Part I of the report, the principles of command and the means of commanding the armed forces. And also I provided an extract of the VJ Manual of Command and Control in Part I describing just how complex military operations are and the nature of commanding them, and from that make the assessment that for units to be engaged on this scale in Kosovo required that they be operating under a common plan. Operations have to be coordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Coo. You have just uncovered the fact that in Kosovo the police corps was in existence. That is no secret. The Pristina Corps did exist, does exist, and its area of responsibility was the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. What's that got to do with your observation, the one you made just now? So what if the Pristina Corps exists? And even if secretariats of internal affairs exist and the police force exists. Of course the police force exists. What then? What are you trying to say? What's it all about? The Pristina Corps does exist. The police force does exist. So what?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other components of the chain of command, the Pristina Corps is a regular -- makes regular appearances in documentation such as orders, orders concerning activities in Kosovo. It also issues orders, and such orders are provided in some of the references in my report. Similarly, the MUP staff in Kosovo appears in operational-related documentation including one we saw of the -- or the MUP in general appears in the Joint Command's documentation. The fact that these organisations, these structures at these two levels, both of which, the MUP staff and the Pristina Corps, have areas of responsibility matching the boundaries in Kosovo, the fact that these two organisations are appearing in such documentation, operational orders included, shows that the scope of the operations in Kosovo involved those two levels of command. And to involve those two levels of command in joint operations, or in operations conducted individually by the VJ and the MUP - but in this case we're discussing a common plan - requires that those operations, those joint operations, be coordinated, and coordination has to come at a high level for those units or command structures at those two levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Coo. I hope you followed the testimony here of General Sir Peter de la Billiere. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you remember, then, that he indicated the importance of mutual cooperation in the field between the military authorities, the civilian authorities, the police, in this case, and he mentioned that in a positive sense, said that that kind of cooperation was indispensable. A representative of the federal government, the government of Serbia, the whole government of the province of Kosovo itself in which, by the way, the Serbs were a minority and was composed of all the ethnic groups, the police, the army, and what you call a Joint Command, in fact represents their mutual cooperation and communication amongst themselves and no kind of command within a chain of command. And to refresh your memory, let me remind you with respect to that assertion that you yourself, I think in paragraph 18, in fact, talk about this when you refer to their coordination. And you say that this command responsibility did not replace the responsibility and authorisation within the chain of command of the army and the Ministry of the Interior. Is that right or is it not?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's a lot to comment on in that. I can begin with I do recall General Sir Peter de la Billiere commenting that -- specifically he used the term, if I my recollection is correct, "coordination" rather than "cooperation" is important between armed organisations. In the VJ doctrine, coordination and cooperation are distinguished by, one, having a command -- involving a command relationship, and that is coordination. The existence, the comment in paragraph 18, I don't recall where in the report, but referring to the Joint Command not supplanting the internal chains of command of the VJ and the MUP, is consistent with the remainder of my report and I think with General de la Billiere's testimony, but that comment refers to the fact that, from my review of what documentation relates to the joint command, it had a coordination role. It also had executive authority because, as I've mentioned, it issued commands which the VJ was bound to abide by, as one document, again in my report, a 1998 125th Brigade document refers to -- orders its sub-units to abide by a Joint Command order. There are other references to Joint Command orders and, therefore, executive authority. But in the case of the MUP and the VJ retaining their internal chains of command, I think that's only common sense. It doesn't mean that those chains of command operated independently of one another. It means that the VJ retained its own mechanisms for reporting along its chain of command to its various commanders at the various levels, all the way up, as did the MUP. The Joint Command brought these two chains of commands together and was responsible for ensuring that they operated in conjunction with one another in a coordinated fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I'm talking about. It is not in the chain of command, it is a form of coordination of civilian, police, and other authorities which, within that coordination, cannot step outside the framework of their own competencies within the frame of their own chain of command. All they can do is exchange information and coordinate, dovetail their activities in order to avoid any unfortunate events taking place, such as being killed by their own crossfire, et cetera. But they nonetheless remain within their own foreseen chains of command. Is that clear or is it not? And I quoted the passage from your report in order to assert that particular viewpoint, because you, too, you yourself found, even if this was done in a fairly amateurish way, that they did retain their own internal chains of command. Is that so, Mr. Coo?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did, as I said, retain their own internal chains of command and means of functioning, but they --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish. You put a long question to him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's just repeating what he's already stated, Mr. May, and you're clipping my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him finish. You repeat often enough. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those two chains of command were quite clearly integrated in some fashion with the Joint Command, and the Joint Command, as I said, had executive authority and it was acting on, or it had links -- it certainly had links to the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any order by the Joint Command that was signed? Is there a commander of this Joint Command? If there is a command, then you must have a commander of that command. So did you come across any document at all which would indicate that this was not a form of cooperation and coordination but that it was in fact the issuance of an order signed by a commander of a Joint Command and, therefore, the existence of a commander of such a Joint Command? Did you ever come across anything like that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen an order signed by a commander of the Joint Command, but that doesn't mean they don't exist. What I have seen is documentation referring to orders issued by the Joint Command. And two that I can recollect are one document from the Supreme Command that was mentioned at -- that was exhibited, I think, at the end of this morning, during the state of war, had at the top the word "link" and a reference to a Joint Command order issued shortly before that Supreme Command order. Also, again I mentioned this minutes ago, in 1998, July - and this is in my document where I cover the joint command - the 125th Brigade of the VJ ordered its sub-units not to act without the order of the Joint Command. And that, to me, shows executive authority over operations of the VJ and the MUP by the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Quite the contrary. What I'm doing and what -- and I precisely consider that because you are not competent to make these assessments, that you were drawing the wrong conclusions from papers which are fairly correct. Let me just find the order that you have just highlighted. Mr. Nice said he has some new pages. I have a new set of documents where that is to be found. Just one moment. Let me just find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Maybe it's 245.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you can see, the head of staff of the Supreme Command refers to the commander of the 3rd Army and not any kind of Joint Command. And he is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have it. We can't go on without the witness having it and the Court having it. Wait a moment. Exhibit 323, I think he must have in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see the number 323, but it is K022-8659. That is the number of the page. K022-8659.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could read the title of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the top it says, "The staff of the Supreme Command, the Sector for Operational Staff Matters, the Operational Department," and then 17th of April, 1999 is the command post. And it says, "To the command of the 3rd Army, to the commander in person."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's Prosecution Exhibit 323, tab 3. Right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, is it clear to you, Mr. Coo, that the staff of the Supreme Command communicates down the vertical line towards a step -- one step lower down? That is to say, the command of the 3rd Army or, rather, it communicates with the commander of the 3rd Army and not with any imaginary commander who doesn't exist, some imaginary Joint Command commander. Now, is it logical to you that the head of staff of the Supreme Command relates to the most superior officer in the area in that terrain and not somebody who is not the most senior? So he is looking at the vertical chain of command and is addressing himself to the commander of the 3rd army. So is it clear to you that this precisely confirms that what they call Joint Command in fact represents a form of coordination and not commanding in the chain of command? Had it been the command within the chain of command, then the head of staff of the Supreme Command would probably have written an objection and remark, the type that is expressed in this letter, and he would have addressed it to the commander of a Joint Command. But as in the absence of that, as that person does not exist, he couldn't have sent a letter in that way but what he is doing is referring himself to his most superior, that is to say, the commander. When I say that, I mean the Supreme Commander who is the superior officer, most superior officer up the next step in the chain of command. Is that clear to you? And what he is doing is he is suggesting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We're going to have a question after this. You've been going for two minutes without any form of question. I'm going to interrupt you. It's the witness giving evidence, not you. Mr. Coo, what is suggested so far is that this shows a vertical chain of command. Do you agree with that assessment or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this does show the exercise of the VJ's vertical chain of command. On top of that, or in addition to that, it shows the relationship between the VJ's vertical chain of command and the entity known as the Joint Command. And as I stressed, the reference is to a Joint Command order and orders are executive documents. And the VJ Manual on Command and Control and my own military experience, it's evident that orders are executive documents, and I can only conclude on the basis of that information that the Joint Command issued an executive document. And I -- I interpret this communication from the Supreme Command Staff to the 3rd Army command as having a basis in something that the 3rd Army had provided to -- or something that the Joint Command had provided to the 3rd Army, or some reaction on the part of the 3rd Army to the Joint Command. And that reaction seems to have been a plan. And this, to me, looks like the Supreme Command commenting on offering its views on the 3rd Army's plan and making some recommendations on adjustments to that plan. But I think, in the end, it shows a link between the Joint Command, the Supreme Command Staff, and the 3rd Army, with some executive authority at specific levels in that link.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Coo, is it clear that this is crystal clear communication between the Supreme Command and the next level down, that is to say, the command of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, on the basis of a Joint Command document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not on the basis of but related to some conclusion that can be called an order mistakenly here. However, since you have the opportunity of getting all documents from the current authorities, why don't you look at that too? Then you will see that this is no executive order, this is a form of coordination. Why did you not ask to have a look at those documents? Because here, this is obviously some kind of activity that is supposed to destroy some forces that are under blockade, and it says here such a deployment of forces that are under blockade it is hard to achieve, et cetera, et cetera, and then there is also an objection to the fact that the forces are under blockade, and this has nothing to do whatsoever with an executive order, because an executive order can go from the Supreme Command to the command of the army to the command of the corps, and so on and so forth, and further down the vertical line, which was not disrupted anywhere. Did you see anywhere - you've had a look at so many documents - that the chain of command was disrupted anywhere?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've seen no evidence of disruption of the chains of command I've described in the report. I -- I think the cover --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on, in order to save time.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I should finish my answer, Your Honour, with a statement to the effect of from the documentation that I reviewed, the Joint Command had a coordination role. "Coordination" in VJ doctrine has command implications. Furthermore, to become involved in the types of things that the Joint Command was involved in - VJ and MUP operations - and to issue the types of documents that it was issuing, namely orders, among others, it would have to have a degree of authority, and my assessment is it would have some degree of command authority, and I've shown its relationship in the report to the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That is your assumption. But it would be very useful if you would have at least one document, one order, that would confirm that assumption of yours. As for coordination, you heard from General de la Billiere what it means and how useful and necessary it is to have coordination between civilian authorities and also the military and police authorities in a given area. That is to say, all authorities in a given area. Did you bear in mind, when making this analysis, that the entire functioning that refers to coordination, orders, operations, that it is all linked to the obligation of the army of Yugoslavia and the police, that is to say the armed forces, and you have read the constitution, with their constitutional obligation and duty to defend the sovereignty, territorial integrity, independence of the country, as the armed forces in any other country would, and that this was a case of mass terrorism and, at the same time, an aggression launched by NATO against the territory of the entire country? Did you bear that in mind when presenting this view of yours? Did you bear in mind these circumstances which I also believe are quite relevant, Mr. Coo?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In very general terms, that was not within the scope of my report. In one of my conclusions or one of my sections with -- entitled "Conclusions," I stated that in relation to the subordination issue of VJ to MUP that perhaps the vigour with which the VJ seemed to be pursuing subordination of the MUP to the VJ in a different manner in which it existed already, that perhaps the VJ was doing that because of the NATO threat, and the reason why the VJ would want the subordination adjusted is perhaps because the tempo of operations and the scope of operations with a NATO ground attack would change significantly and the VJ wanted greater control over MUP units in combat operations. That was by no means a statement that the VJ-MUP relationship was an independent one and that there wasn't a command relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But if we are going to dwell on that, I should think that you do assume that this resubordination in the zone of combat operations does not mean resubordinating the Ministry of the Interior to the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia. Some authorities and units during a certain combat assignment, combat task, in the zone of combat operations are resubordinated to military commanders precisely in order to avoid accidents or mistakes or any deviation from the single effort to react to terrorist forces and so on. So there is a series of activities undertaken by the Ministry of the Interior that has nothing to do with the military, and there are so many things that are done by the military that have nothing to do with the police. And in this case, the police forces are resubordinated to the military commanders in the zone of combat operations while combat operations are taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can't go on in this way. Now, what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is that logical, Mr. Coo?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Internal Affairs, according to the legislation and doctrine, would not be in its entirety subordinated to the VJ. Subordination, as outlined in Article 17 of the law on defence, is for combat operations. But you should also look at that in relation to, as the preceding Article, Article 16, which states that the VJ -- and I can't remember the exact wording but it's along the lines of the VJ unifies all armed organisations in defence of the country. And an element of that, at least one element, or more, in fact, are presented in my report in relation to the local defence concept, the imposition of VJ command over local defence during a state of war. And that came out of a Pec military sector document from 30 March 1999. So in short, no, there isn't a blanket subordination of internal affairs to the VJ. But I would suggest that, with respect, the two articles in particular of the law on defence are looked at on the subject of subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I've been indicating, Mr. Coo. I think that at least that has been made clear now. Tell me, please, among the documents that you examined, did you have the directive for the engagement of the army of Yugoslavia in defence from NATO aggression which I assume that you, as a military expert of that side across the well, would have to have had, because I got that directive from them. "Directive for the Engagement of the Army of Yugoslavia on Defence from NATO Aggression" which contains 12 pages and which was sent on the 9th of April, 1999, to the commands of the strategic groups. Did you also study that directive as another very important document, because the Supreme Command addresses the strategic groups through a directive, that is to say the armies, the air force, the anti-aircraft defence, the navy, and gives them combat tasks. Did you study that directive?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've seen that directive. It sounds very familiar. I think it was in a batch of documents given to us recently. I did not choose to comment on it or include it in my report because I don't think it falls within the scope of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Explain the following to me: Mr. Coo, what is the logic? I'm looking at this list now, this list of documents that were given to General Sir Peter de la Billiere, and then it says pre-trial brief, number 1. First document, the main document, that is to say the indictment. Then instructions to the 4th Corps command, and so on and so forth. And then attack order, brigades, then an analysis of combat operations, of combat groups, that is to say, a few of these lower-ranking orders. And then the Yugoslav law on the army of Yugoslavia, the Yugoslav law on defence. The army of Yugoslavia, the command control manual, and so on. How, then -- on the basis of what did you conclude that it was more important to give such documents rather than this document which is called the Directive of the Supreme Command and that contains a great deal of information for drawing conclusions concerning matters that you would like to draw conclusions on?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm thinking of the same 9th of April document, it wasn't available at the time that General de la Billiere wrote his report. As to having given it to him for -- during his testimony, that wouldn't be my decision, that would be the decision of the legal people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have the document available if the Chamber wants it to be produced, or if the accused does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is different. Who decided that the Directive of the Supreme Command - how should I put this? - be selected in such a way that it does not belong to the things that you do analyse, whereas these other things that are of far lesser importance are considered to be relevant and significant? You say that you were not the one who decided about that. Who did?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP COO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this document came to us after my report was written and submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Since we haven't heard about it before, perhaps you could just briefly introduce it, Mr. Coo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I explain the position? These were documents that arrived very recently, translated extremely recently. This was one of a number that were provided to the accused post haste, as I said the other day, under Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Since it's been referred to, let's deal with it now and we can have it exhibited. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, looking at this, it's -- again it's issued by the Supreme Command Staff on the 9th of April to, and that section is not filled in. I can't say why. Perhaps this copy wasn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. My question is not who issued it and when. That is all written on the document itself. It's not necessary to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Milosevic. You have introduced this document. It's right, if you want us to consider it, that we should look at it, and I asked the witness -- I have asked the witness to introduce it briefly. That is all he's doing. Yes, Mr. Coo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I go to the last page of the document to see who it was addressed to, it shows that it was addressed to the three armies within the VJ and the air defence forces. And I don't know what "RM Command" is. The contents of the document, in a quick review, seems to -- it seems to be -- it's a directive for how the addressees should engage themselves in general terms against the expected threat, and part of that threat is NATO. And they list in -- I think they're listing, in sub-heading 2, aggression against the FRY, what precisely what that aggression is comprised of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We will give it the next Prosecution exhibit number so they can stay together.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 324.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was not who the document was addressed to, because that's what is written on it. It's addressed to the strategic groups. And this "RM" that you do not know what it means, means the navy, "Ratna Mornarica." So it was sent to the air force and to the army and also to the navy. So it is also addressed to the three armies. If do you not know, Mr. Coo, these three armies and the navy and the air force are strategic groups within the army of Yugoslavia, and the Supreme Command gives them tasks through this directive. After all, that's what we discussed with General de la Billiere. My question was why such an important document, why such an important document was not given to your military expert, General de la Billiere, in order for him to have a look at it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given an answer. He's answered the question. He said it wasn't available. Now, we'll adjourn now because it's the time, and resume tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 11th day of September, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
